newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy government adds expiring decrees to budget.
newsitem.headline: Italy government adds expiring decrees to budget.

text.p: The Italian government has added six cabinet decrees, which were on the verge of expiring, to the 1997 budget package to ensure that they pass swiftly into law, a coalition official said on Wednesday.
Opposition parties, which are boycotting the budget debate in protest at government demands for special powers to dictate policy without recourse to parliament, lambasted the decision.

The opposition walkout has helped smooth the budget's path through parliament, and the government, taking advantage of the unexpected calm, added the decrees, which concern financial issues, to the budget bill late on Tuesday.

Under a recent court ruling, the government is barred from continuing the traditional practice of re-issuing expiring decrees. Instead they have to be converted into law by parliament within 60 days or dropped.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi has already called two confidence votes to ram expiring decrees into law and a further three do-or-die votes are due in the upper house (Senate) later on Wednesday.
Among the decrees attached to the budget was one covering an amnesty on illegal building work and another on an end-of-year financial package introduced in 1995 by then prime minister Lamberto Dini.
The government tried to attach a much larger number of decrees to the budget on Tuesday night, but the speaker of the lower house, Luciano Violante, said they were not all admissable.
Tieing the decrees to the budget enables the government to keep potentially dangerous confidence votes to a minimum.
Leader of the hardright National Alliance Gianfranco Fini criticised the move.

"This time the government has shown itself to be utterly without shame," he told reporters. "There is no precedent for this kind of behaviour and shows both the level of arrogance and desperation within the majority."
The undersecretary for parliamentary relations, Giorgio Bogi, told reporters he did not want to get involved in a fight with the opposition.

"The government understands the gravity of the situation," he said, but added: "There are a number of decrees which concern state accounts and we have tried to reach an agreement with the opposition. This has not happened.
"The government did not want to attach (the decrees) to the budget but had no other option," he added.

Parliament has yet to vote on the new amendments. Final approval on the budget in the lower house of parliament is due by the end of Thursday after which it passes to the upper house (Senate) for ratification. -- Rome newsroom +396 6782501
